newsitem.title: USA: AA strike seen hitting jet fuel prices.
newsitem.headline: AA strike seen hitting jet fuel prices.

text.p: The price of jet fuel in the United States will probably slump sharply if pilots of American Airlines carry out a threatened strike at midnight Friday, industry executives said.
American Airlines buys 130,000 to 140,000 barrels per day of jet fuel in the U.S., nearly 10 percent of total U.S. demand.
"If AA walks and there are 140,000 barrels per day that aren't going to be used, we will see depressed prices," said a fuel trader for a rival U.S. airline.
An easing in jet fuel costs, which typically represent 10 to 15 percent of a carrier's costs, would come as welcome relief for the rest of the industry after a time of high prices.
"Jet fuel prices have been killing the airlines especially now since it is the season when airlines have been giving away tickets," said Tom Manning of energy consultant Purvin & Gertz Inc.
Jet prices shot up 50 percent during third quarter 1996 to more than 75 cents a gallon, leading some international carriers to slap fuel surcharges on air fares.

Pilots of American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, have threatened to strike at midnight Friday if their demand for an 11.5 percent pay raise is not met. Also at issue is AA's plan for its regional carrier, American Eagle, to use jets flown by lower-paid members of another union.

Early Thursday, AA's chairman said he was unsure a strike by the pilots could be avoided. Those comments came less than 24 hours after a pilot's spokesman said there has been no progress in talks and a "strike is more likely than not."
Jet fuel traders said AA is likely to sell off its supply rather than store it, given the high premium for prompt delivery which currently prevails, making the cost of storage prohibitive.
Also, AA is known for keeping lean stocks, making it more likely that its extra barrels will come onto the spot market, traders said.

"There are not too many airlines out there right now who want to store barrels in this backwardation," said a Georgia-based jet fuel trader, referring to the two cents a gallon premium for prompt versus March delivery.
One factor that may hold up prices, however, is whether other carriers can pick up the slack for any flights cancelled by AA.
Philip Verleger, chief economist at Charles River Associates, said some carriers could reinstate midnight flights or increase their load, given availability of crews.

"It's obvious a strike will depress prices but we still don't yet know what the other airlines can do," said Verleger, noting this is busy travel season for tourists who have already locked in discount AA tickets.
